title: Gateless Barrier, Case 32: The Buddha Responds to an Outsider
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk emphasizes the importance of embracing uncertainty and silence in order to cultivate courage and wisdom. In a world filled with constant talking and distraction, it's essential to practice "emptiness" by letting go of all views and acknowledging the unknown nature of reality. By doing so, we can develop the strength and clarity needed to navigate life's challenges, including those presented by uncertainty and fear.

sentences.text: Good to see everybody in this remote way.
Good evening.
These darn Zen koans keep making sense, so here's another one: Nomon koan case 32.
*An outsider said to the Buddha, "I do not ask for the spoken.
I do not ask for the unspoken."
The world honored one just sat still.
The honored one praised him saying, "The world honored one with his great compassion and mercy has opened the clouds to my delusion and enabled me to enter the way."
Then he made bows and took his leave.
Ananda asked, "What did the outsider realize that made him praise you so?"
Buddha said, "He is like a fine horse who runs even at the shadow of the whip."*
*An outsider said to the Buddha, "I do not ask for the spoken.
I do not ask for the unspoken."
The world honored one just sat still.
And the outsider praised him saying, "The world honored one with his great compassion and mercy has opened the clouds of my delusion and enabled me to enter the way."
Then he made bows and took his leave.
Later, Ananda asked, "What did the outsider realize to make him praise you so?"
And the Buddha said, "He is like a fine horse who runs even at the shadow of the whip."*
*I do not ask for the spoken.
I do not ask for the unspoken.* Boy, it seems like the environment is full of the spoken, even though most of us are spending more time alone or just with one or two people.
The world is somehow full of the spoken: daily press briefings, governors giving speeches about new guidelines, pundits, columnists, friends, neighbors, calling your family.
Everybody's talking, talking, talking.
So much spoken.
So maybe we do need the unspoken too.
Maybe we need silence.
The speaking delineates the world of knowing things that you know.
And there's so much always that seems to be unknown, even really important things.
Speech can point to the unknown too, so the spoken can speak of the unspoken.
We can say that we don't know, we really don't know.
But the mind wants so much to say and hear more, wants to know, doesn't it?
I read that, I heard that, I believe, I predict, expert opinion, non-expert opinion.
I was thinking, wouldn't it be great if we, during this time, had a daily national minute of silence, or an hour of silence?
And maybe we're doing our bit a little more than usual in the meditation communities to have daily silence.
I really appreciate today.
I got to start the day pretty much with sangha, with our 7 a.m. sit here, and end the day with sangha at 7 p.m.
It's wonderful to have the unspoken in our lives as well: a time for everyone to sit and breathe and stop.
But only silence wouldn't be right either.

The stranger, this visiting monk or philosopher, somebody who visited the Buddha from outside the community, wherever he was from, asked this: I do not ask for the spoken, I do not ask for the unspoken.
Not just speaking, not just silence.
What really makes sense?
Nagarjuna, who was a great Buddhist philosopher from the third century, wrote endlessly about emptiness using lots of different mechanisms and metaphors and language.
And this is new to me, I just read this, that one of the things he said is, emptiness is a departure from all views.
A departure from all views.
So maybe a great service we can offer ourselves and our friends and our neighbors, our family, is to practice with that somehow.
Departure from all views.
To be like a holder of not knowing and deeply acknowledging how hard that is, not just glib or religious about it or something.
It's not easy to have a departure from all views, for us.
Maybe we really need that right now.
Maybe we really need a sense of the potentiality and the fluidity and the unknowability that emptiness reminds us about, which is how things actually are.
So that we can really acknowledge that we're afraid, that there's so much uncertainty.
And it's really obvious now that that's the case.
Of course it's always the case, but it's so obvious now.
But the thing that we get mixed up about, I think here's where we can really make a contribution.
I think the thing that we all get mixed up about, all of us being humans, is we get a little confused about fear and uncertainty.
We think it's the uncertainty that's causing the fear.
So if we could just have certainty, we wouldn't have fear.
It seems to be looking at it a little bit the wrong way around, since uncertainty is an essential part of reality.
So we're not going to get rid of it.
Fear is somehow pointing to something else, something deeper.
We're looking in the wrong places.
Because uncertainty is how things are, right?
This is reality.
And so much we don't know about this obvious pointer to uncertainty, the epidemic, the pandemic.
We don't know when it's going to peak.
We don't know if there even will be a back to normal on the other side, right?
We don't know that.
We talk that way.
I talk that way: once things are back to normal.
We don't know that.
We know the change is happening and will happen.
We don't know what kind of changes.
We don't know what's going to happen with the physical world, or if the food and toilet paper will hold up or run out.
How much unemployment there will be.
We don't know any of this.
Will there be restaurants still?
New restaurants?
How many people will physically survive?
We don't know.
So maybe as practitioners, we can really practice feeling that tug towards wanting to know, wanting to have an opinion, wanting to have a prediction, a guess.
And maybe we can hold the line a little bit and rest in uncertainty and honor that there is a healing there.
There's actually healing in uncertainty, in openness, in emptiness, and the courage to just be in this moment, right?
In this unfolding, in this not knowing.
And to really acknowledge that that's not an easy thing.
It requires practice and strength and courage, but it can also feel really good, oddly, when we give ourselves over to that, this incredible sense of potential.
So it's interesting, this phrase from Nagarjuna, emptiness as departure from all views.
In the story, the Buddha didn't express any views.
He just sat.
In one of the translations, instead of saying the Buddha just sat there or sat there quietly, one of the translations said the Buddha changed position to sit correctly.
So maybe he demonstrated, oh, now it's time to really practice [unclear: "sasa"] and to really be embodied, to really be an expression of awakening.
Although actually I checked the Chinese and it doesn't really say that, so I don't know why the one translation said that.
It says he sat there quietly, no speaking, sitting, or something like that.
But in Nagarjuna, after he says emptiness is departure from all views, then he goes on to say, but those who hold to the view of emptiness cannot be saved.
He's a pull-the-rug-out kind of teacher.
Emptiness is departure from all views, but those who hold to the view of emptiness cannot be saved.
There's no one practice or one understanding or one way of being.
Just being quiet all the time won't cut it either.
It's like the story last week: we can't just go straightforward.

We have to have some feeling and understanding and subtlety and keep studying and learning how to go forward, how to be free from views, how to be open to uncertainty, how to be with fear and all the feelings in a wise way.
In the story, the Buddha's ability to hold space really seemed to help the outsider to just sit.
And the outsider was really delighted, really helped, him or her.
The outsider said, *the world honored one with great compassion and mercy has opened the clouds of my delusion.* That's a good phrase, right?
We're clouded, clouded by delusion, *and enabled me to enter the way.*
Then he made his bows and took his leave.
I think this is remarkably apt to our current situation.
We really can, I think, help to open the clouds of delusion and help others enter the way by holding space: six feet of space, meditation space, not-knowing space, soft-with-our-views space.
We're learning and understanding as best we can, trying to get accurate information and sharing it, and when we encounter inaccurate information, for sure, speaking and not speaking.
But can we hold the space?
It really might be that this confusing time is an incredibly rich time for practice.
In my day job at Mindfulness Northwest, we've been hurriedly trying to shift everything online, because we run these programs with people in person, just like we do at Red Cedar, right?
And suddenly you can't do that.
When we started to do that, I found myself holding these views: oh, this isn't going to work, this is too weird.
But so far people seem to be really showing up.
There's a lot of interest.
The numbers initially are looking promising.
So maybe that's true for all kinds of practice-oriented living, which you could also call true living or grounded living or open living.
Maybe this calamity is also a huge opportunity.
The Chinese word for danger has two characters, and one means danger and one means opportunity.
So it's a danger-opportunity, a time for us really to practice.
It's wonderful that we're starting to figure out how to stay connected and keep practicing together online.
And I know that we're all trying to practice at home.
But then the last part of the story is remarkably relevant to the exact situation that we're in.
So then Ananda shows up later.
Maybe he was there all the time.
I remember Ananda, Buddha's cousin and attendant, a brilliant guy with a perfect memory.
He got top grades at school, but somehow he has trouble quite getting it.
He's a sort of foil in the Zen tradition.
Poor guy.
I think he was a really sweet guy, too.
So he has his usual question, which more or less always amounts to, huh?
Ananda asks at the end of the story, "What did the outsider realize to make him praise you so?"
He didn't say, "What did you say?
What does that mean, what you said?"
He said, "What did the outsider realize?"

And the Buddha replied, *He's like a fine horse who runs even at the shadow of the whip.* This fine horse who runs at the shadow of the whip is a reference to an early Buddhist teaching that Suzuki Roshi was fond of quoting in *Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind*.
It's a teaching from the Anguttara Nikaya, from the early Pali Canon.
You don't even know which book it's in.
I can't pronounce it right now.
It's a teaching called the Patoda Sutra, and a patoda is like a stick you use to whack an animal.
Here it's translated as a whip, the shadow of the whip.
So here's a short version of this sutra, which is actually longer and more repetitive than this.
This is pretty interesting, though.
*The one who learns that someone in another village is about to die and reflects on the transient nature of all life is like a horse who runs when it sees the shadow of the whip.
The one who learns that someone in her own village is about to die and reflects on the transient nature of life is like a horse who runs when it feels the whip on its hair.*
*The one who learns that someone in his own family is about to die and reflects on the transient nature of life is like a horse who runs when it feels the whip on its flesh.
The one who learns that she herself is about to die and reflects on the transient nature of all life is like a horse who runs when it feels the whip in its bones.*
Let me just read that again.
You'll see my notes later on.
It's easier to see this visually too.
*The one who learns that someone in another village is about to die and reflects on the transient nature of all life is like a horse who runs when it sees the shadow of a whip.
The one who learns that someone in her own village is about to die and reflects on the transient nature of all life is like a horse who runs when it feels the whip on its hair.*
*The one who learns that someone in his own family is about to die and reflects on the transient nature of all life is like the horse who runs when it feels the whip on its flesh.
The one who learns that she herself is about to die and reflects on the transient nature of all life is like a horse who runs when it feels the whip in its bones.*
So I think this is an exact description of how we respond to the coronavirus, isn't it?
Maybe it happened this way in waves too, but at first the virus was in another village, right?
Off in China.
I'm sure we were all reading about this and wondering about it and worried about it, but maybe we didn't feel it yet or really understand it in a deeper way.
We didn't notice the shadow of the whip.
And now it's in our village.
It's in our country, in our county.
So we're feeling the whip on our skin, getting it a little more deeply.
And by now we probably all know somebody, either directly or one degree removed: a friend of a friend, a family member of a friend, or a family member of ourselves, who has the virus.
So we're feeling the whip on the flesh, right?
Sinking in.
And sooner or later some of us, or some that we know, will ourselves have the virus, will ourselves be about to die, or we pray we'll recover.
And then we'll really understand deeply the transient nature of all life, right?
That everything comes and goes.
Our species is not guaranteed.
None of our lives are guaranteed.
The only thing uncertain is when, right?
So isn't that wild?
The coin that happened to be up next referred to this story.
And one of the things about this story, though, is that it's easy to feel a little guilty, right?
I should have been paying more attention.
I should have noticed the shadow of the whip.
I should have known.
I should have noticed the shadow of the whip.
I should have known.
Hopefully people on the national level, we want them to feel that way a little bit, like we should have been stockpiling better and organizing and preparing for all this.
It's easy for us to feel blaming of those in power who didn't notice the shadow of the whip, right?
Now we'll understand that the shadow of this whip is always there.
Always there.
But Suzuki Roshi tries to encourage us when he talks about this story.
He says it's okay that we're slow.
It's okay that we're a little thick.
In the context of Zen training, it's okay to be the slow horse that needs to feel this in our bones.
So here's a couple of paragraphs from *Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind*, and then I'll close the talk.
We can discuss all this a little bit, or whatever else is on your mind.
This is Suzuki Roshi.
*It's said that there are four kinds of horses: excellent ones, good ones, poor ones, and bad ones.
The best horse will run slow and fast, right and left, at the driver's will, well before it sees the shadow of the whip.
The second best will run as well as the first one does, but just before the whip reaches its skin.
The third one will run when it feels the pain on its body.
The fourth one will run only after the pain penetrates to the marrow of its bones.*
*You can imagine how difficult it is for the fourth one to learn how to run.
When we hear this story, almost all of us want to be the best horse.
If it's impossible to be the best one, we want to be the second best.
That is, I think, the usual understanding of this story and of Zen and of life.
You may think that when you sit in Zazen, you'll find out whether you are one of the best horses or one of the worst ones.
Here, however, there is some misunderstanding of Zen.
If you think that the aim of Zen practice is to train you to become the best horse, you have a big problem.
That's not the right understanding.*
*If you practice Zen in the right way, it does not matter whether you are the best horse or the worst horse.
When you consider the mercy of Buddha, how do you think Buddha will feel about the four kinds of horses?
You'll have more sympathy for the worst one than the best one.
When you're determined to practice Zazen with the great mind of Buddha, you'll find the worst horse is the most valuable one.
In your very first imperfections, you'll find the basis for your firm way-seeking mind.
In your very imperfection, you will find the basis for your firm way-seeking mind.
Those who can sit perfectly physically usually take more time to attain the true way of Zen, the actual feeling of Zen, the marrow of Zen.
But those who find great difficulty in practicing Zen will find more meaning in it.*
So I think that sometimes the best horse may be the worst horse, and the worst horse may be the best one.
That's encouraging if you feel like a crummy meditator, huh?
That's the best way to be.
Once you get it, you'll have it.
The last thing I want to mention, actually I want to mention one more thing, and we'll stop, is that I was watching a recent Dharma talk by Jack Kornfield.
I don't often watch or listen to talks, but I was glad to watch this one.
Jack has a good way about him.
Among many things, he quoted Thich Nhat Hanh talking about the boat people fleeing from southern Vietnam after the war there.
They were fleeing reprisals from the new communist government.
This was in the mid-70s, started in '75 and peaked in '78, '79.
People were piling into little fisherman's boats and heading off towards Thailand or Hong Kong without decent supplies or enough fuel or anything like that, or working motors.
I just read up on this to remind myself: mostly they didn't really expect to make it all the way to Thailand or Hong Kong or Singapore.
They'd just cruise out into the busy shipping lanes and pray for rescue.
Can you imagine?
And if that wasn't bad enough, pirates figured out this was happening and started preying on these folks.
A lot of them were attacked by pirates.
The statistics are truly frightening.
You can read the Wikipedia article if you want to know.
So many attacks and rapes and murders and theft.
And Thich Nhat Hanh was saying it was so much harder, so, so much harder if they panicked in the middle of this calamitous situation.
They were much more likely to survive if they could somehow stay calm, hold their seats in the middle of that.

He said that on each boat, if there was just one person who really could do that, who really could stay grounded, who really could stay awake, who could keep breathing even in the middle of a frightening, frightening situation like that, then it would go much better.
Everyone else would feel much better.
So Jack Kornfield's suggesting, and I'm suggesting, maybe we could be like that person: a calm person in the boat helping everyone around us, on this lifeboat of earth, if you will.
Then maybe this really is not just a time to practice, but a time to be a little more willing to share the practice in whatever way we can.
Whether that's overt or just through the example of our life, through offering space, through kindness, through patience, through helping others.
And I'm glad to say that we've constellated a really strong Red Cedar membership support group.
A wonderful core of four people, and they'll be reaching out to you soon to ask what you need and ask how you can help.
So we can help each other within the Sangha for sure.
Good practice, and we need that.
But of course, much wider than that, giving space with six feet.
I went on a little walk today, and I kept wanting to say good job to people as they stepped over to the far side of the road, the trail.
And by the way, if the trails are too crowded, I have a tip for you on exercise.
Come to downtown Bellingham, and there's nobody.
You can just walk right through town.
I walked here, and I only encountered like four people on the whole walk, which is interesting and creepy, isn't it?
So that's tonight's talk.
Do not ask for the spoken.
Do not ask for the unspoken.
What can we offer?
What can we offer?
Can we be whatever horse we are, whether we and others need the shadow of the whip or really feel it in our bones?
Sooner or later, we're all going to feel it in our bones.
Thank you very much.
*May our intention equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.*
I thought for the first part of discussion, last time we went all around, which was wonderful to hear from everybody, and of course took quite a while.
So I thought we might try tonight to make use of the small group feature this thing has, which are called breakout rooms.
I'm going to click a few buttons and you're going to see an invitation to join a breakout room.
So if you please click that.
Then you'll find yourself in a group of three or four people and just have some discussion time there.

I think I'll unmute you all and then I'll do the group thing.
You're unmuted.
Now breakout rooms.
Hopefully they also work smoothly.
I'll see you in 10. [unclear: "She just raised on adventure."] Oh, God.
Okay.
Let me try.
You should see an invitation to join your room.
Once randomly end up with.
